name: Perma-smile theory

lead: Perma-smile theory is the idea that a habitual, slight smile changes how the eye area and midface look. Proponents on looksmax.org say a smile raises the lower eyelid and cheek, which can cover visible white below the iris (scleral show) and make the eyes look more appealing.

The theory is mostly about presentation rather than bone structure: users describe holding a mild smile in photos, or warming up the smile muscles so the face rests in a friendlier expression. No published study has tested whether a constant smile reshapes the face over time.

paras: Practitioners describe keeping a slight smile in photos and conversation, and one forum user describes exaggerating a smile for about 30 seconds so that the smile muscles feel engaged and the face looks happier, with the effect fading in about 15 minutes.
No physical risks are reported for smiling. Forum discussions of the theory sometimes carry harsh insults between users, which are not part of the practice itself.

lead: Perma-smile theory is a looksmaxxing concept holding that a constant slight smile, or a face that rests in a smile-like position, improves the look of the eye area and cheeks. The original thread on looksmax.org argues that smiling raises the under-eye region slightly and can hide scleral show, the visible white beneath the iris, which the poster says noticeably improves the eye area.[1]

Users apply the idea as expression management rather than a procedure. The thread's author says he does not squint or smile in his pictures like other members but finds a slight smile helps, and asks how to look permanently happy; one reply describes an exaggerated smile held for about 30 seconds that leaves the smile muscles engaged for around 15 minutes.[1]

Research on facial expression has examined how smiling affects the person smiling. The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that expressions modulate emotion, and a 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies reported small effects (around d = 0.2).[2] That research concerns mood rather than permanent facial structure, and no published study has examined a perma-smile effect on the eye area.
infobox: Improve eye area and cheek appearance

paras: The theory concerns the interaction between the smile and the eye area. As described by its proponents, smiling lifts the cheeks and lower eyelids, which reduces scleral show and makes protruding or wide eyes appear more flattering.[1]

The idea circulates on looksmax.org in the context of bug-eye or scleral-show concerns. Replies in the originating thread mix practical suggestions with insults, and the one constructive method offered is a brief exaggerated smile that users say leaves the face looking happier for a short time.[1]

The facial feedback hypothesis, rooted in a 1988 pen-in-mouth study, holds that facial expressions influence emotion. A 17-lab replication in 2016 found no systematic effect, while a 2019 meta-analysis of 138 studies found small but robust effects.[2] These studies measure emotional experience, not changes to the appearance of the eye area.
No studies found. Related laboratory work on facial feedback concerns mood rather than eye-area appearance.[2]
